title: Optimize console savings runway & prefetch plan with Northbridge Labs

Customer to run 48h traffic snapshot and share logs
action_items: Maya - send optimized prefetch + batching workbook and pricing by 2026-10-13
Sam - upload sample 48h request traces and traffic heatmap by 2026-10-15

transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-10-11 14:00 UTC | Duration: ~62m | Recording: yes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Evan (Redwood SE), Janelle (Product), Priya (Northbridge CTO), Sam (Northbridge Lead SWE), Aisha (SRE), Tom (Procurement)
Summary: Demo/walkthrough of Redwood Optimize console with emphasis on prefetch (prefix/KV) caching patterns, batching recommendations and cost model scenarios. Goal: validate economics for a 2M monthly token workload and align pilot scope and security checklist.
Topics: optimize console tour, prefetch vs session caching, KV cache TTLs, batching concurrency, latency budgets, hosted vs private inference, SOC2/KMS questions, pilot next steps
-- Transcript body --
[00:00] Maya: okay good afternoon everybody, thanks for joining. quick introductions, i'm maya on the redwood growth team and i'll run the agenda. evan is here to dig into the console and the prefetch/caching sim.
[00:08] Priya: hey yea thanks, i think we're mostly here to understand the unit economics. we've got a lot of user sessions right now, about 2 million tokens a month across our chat assistant and summarization pipeline.
[00:15] Sam: yeah and latencies are sensitive for chat, under 300ms p95 ideally, our cost target is to not exceed current infra spend more than 20%.
[00:22] Evan: cool, that helps. we'll show the optimize console, the prefetch profiles, how prefix/K V cache differs from sessionization, and then run two cost scenarios — conservative and aggressive prefetch.
[00:30] Aisha: quick security callout, we need to know how tokens are stored, if you keep logs or KV entries and how KMS is used.
[00:36] Maya: noted, we'll cover the storage model and KMS integration near the end and share SOC2 docs.
[00:42] 
[01:12] Evan: opening the console — top left is the workload profile. here we ingested a synthetic 48h trace that mirrors northbridge traffic pattern you gave us, spikes around 9am and 6pm UTC, lots of short chats plus longer summarization runs. see the histogram on seq len.
[01:28] Sam: that's close. our real seq len distribution is bimodal so that matters for batching.
[01:34] Evan: yep exactly, bimodal means we can favor micro-batches for short sequences and let longer summarization jobs batch separately or use async throughput. the optimize tab suggests two prefetch profiles: prefix-heavy and conservative.
[01:46] Maya: quick definition for everyone: prefetch here means pre-populating KV cache of commonly-used prefix tokens from history so generation spends less time recomputing attention for the same prefix. sometimes folks call this lookahead or prefix cache.
[01:58] Priya: does prefetch increase KV storage costs? and what's the TTL pattern you'd recommend?
[02:05] Evan: good q. yes you pay for KV lookups and the storage footprint. our cost model has three levers: hit rate, avg tokens saved per hit, and KV pricing (per-lookup + storage). conservative profile assumes 30% hit rate with short TTLs (5 min) to keep storage low; aggressive assumes 65% hit rate with 1 hour TTL and larger storage. we can show the delta.
[02:22] 
[03:40] Evan: switching to the cost sim: baseline (no prefetch) for your 2M tokens/month workload is approx X GPU-hours and estimated $7,800 monthly in inference spend on hosted plan — that's a ballpark from your trace. with conservative prefetch we reduce per-token compute by ~12% and cut cost to about $6,900; aggressive prefetch with higher hits and batching combined reduces ~28% giving ~$5,600. these numbers fold in estimated KV lookup costs (we show as separate line items).
[03:58] Tom: can you break out the lookup math? procurement wants clarity.
[04:03] Evan: sure: lookups are charged as $0.0002 per lookup in hosted — so with aggressive prefetch assuming 1.2 lookups per request average and 65% hit rate you get ~1.56M lookups/mo — that's ~$310. storage is negligible at that scale, like $40/mo for the prefetched entries. compute savings far outweigh that.
[04:20] Sam: ok that's promising. what's the impact on latency? prefetch sounds like it could add lookup latency.
[04:26] Janelle: and also how does this interact with batching and concurrency?
[04:30] Evan: great questions. our default KV lookup adds ~3-6ms p50 and 10-30ms p95 depending on region and if lookups are remote in VPC. but you avoid the expensive attention recompute which saves 60-120ms p95 on long prefixes. so net often improves for long tail. for short messages small overhead may hurt p50 by a few ms but combined with micro-batching you can amortize activation costs.
[04:48] Aisha: in our network we prefer lookups inside VPC, are there known performance differences?
[04:52] Evan: internal VPC deployments (Private) yield lower p95 for KV lookups; hosted cross-region lookups are slightly higher. we can run a quick bench using your test CIDR during pilot.
[05:00] 
[05:42] Priya: can you explain session cache vs prefix KV cache again, because we were debating which to build around.
[05:48] Evan: sure — session cache stores the full user context tokenized and kept warm for active sessions, good for conversational UX with sticky sessions; prefix/KV cache stores recurring prefixes (greetings, system prompts, common completions) keyed for fast reuse across users. session cache is memory-heavy but very low latency for active users; prefix cache trades more lookups but benefits across broader user base. for your heavy short chat load plus repeated system prompts, prefix cache wins economically.
[06:06] Sam: we have many ephemeral sessions though, so session cache hit rate would be low.
[06:09] Maya: yeah that's typical, prefix cache often gives the higher ROI when sessions aren't sticky.
[06:14] 
[06:50] Evan: walking through the optimize console's prefetch policy editor — you can target policies by route, model, and TTL. there's a preview that simulates hit rate based on uploaded traces. you can also set fallback policies to degrade to a smaller model if the cache miss ratio spikes.
[07:04] Priya: interesting, can we use different policies for summarization vs chat?
[07:08] Evan: absolutely, route-level policies recommended. summarization tends to have long sequences so caching prefixes for repeated system prompts is less effective but batching helps. chat benefits more from short prefix caching.
[07:18] 
[08:20] Sam: the batching recommendations — console suggests batch size 16 for short chat, and 32 for medium length, with concurrency target of 8 to keep p95 under 300ms. what's behind those numbers?
[08:28] Evan: it's a scheduler model we built from the runtime: it estimates model throughput per GPU and your sequence length distribution then suggests batch size/concurrency combos to hit latency SLOs. smaller batch sizes reduce latency but lower GPU utilization. the console finds sweet spots given your trace.
[08:40] 
[09:30] Tom: on pricing: if we go dedicated vs hosted how does costing change? procurement wants a side-by-side.
[09:36] Maya: dedicated reserved capacity changes the math — you pay fixed monthly for capacity (better for steady high throughput) and you can reduce per-token compute costs by ~30-45% depending on commit. the console has a dedicated toggle that recomputes break-even points. for your 2M tokens the break-even might be longer than one quarter unless you ramp to sustained higher traffic; we'll show that in the workbook.
[09:56] Priya: so maybe start hosted with prefetch and do a pilot to measure real hit rates before we commit.
[10:02] Evan: that's exactly the recommended path. pilot collects real-world hits and lets us tune TTLs and batching.
[10:08] 
[10:45] Evan: demoing the optimize "what-if" slider — moving prefetch aggressiveness from 0 to 1 and seeing cost curve. notice how KV lookup costs (small) are visually separated and there is an estimated net savings band. also showing the sensitivity table for hit rate +- 10%.
[11:02] Sam: can you export that sensitivity table as CSV? our finance team prefers CSV.
[11:05] Evan: yes export button on top right — we will share the workbook too.
[11:10] 
[12:25] Priya: security again: do prefetched tokens retain PII? how do you scrub?
[12:31] Janelle: good callout — prefetch keys are hashed, and contents stored in encrypted K V with optional redaction rules. you can opt to not cache messages flagged with PII or set TTL to zero. we'll attach the data flow diagram.
[12:45] Aisha: and KMS? we must rotate keys annually and have customer-managed keys.
[12:50] Maya: Redwood supports customer-managed keys via KMS/HSM for Private and Dedicated; hosted also supports bring-your-own-key for enterprise tiers. we'll include integration notes.
[12:58] 
[14:00] Evan: quick technical deep-dive: how the runtime uses prefix cache — at token generation we first check KV by prefix hash, if hit we hydrate KV into the KV cache for the model's runtime, bypassing the early attention recompute. this saves many FLOPS but requires careful cache consistency when you do model rollouts. we have automatic invalidation hooks tied to model version and route changes.
[14:22] Sam: so when we roll a prompt update, invalidations won't create a spike?
[14:26] Evan: we have canary invalidation + staggered TTL drains. plus the console shows projected cold-start penalty during rollout so you can schedule low-traffic windows.
[14:34] 
[15:30] Priya: for pilot scope — what minimal telemetry do you need from us?
[15:33] Evan: sample 48h request traces (request id, route, timestamp, token count, system prompt/hash, response latency), preferably gzipped NDJSON. Sam you'll upload those.
[15:41] Sam: yes we'll do that. we may need a scrub step to anonymize user ids.
[15:44] Maya: that's fine; we only need hashed ids for session affinity analysis.
[15:48] 
[16:58] Janelle: one more console feature — scoring rules for quality/regression: we tie quality metrics to prompt test suites so if prefetch leads to higher ngram drift we alert. we surfaced a sample false-positive scenario where a stale prefix produced a subtle hallucination.
[17:12] Priya: important. we can't accept even small increases in hallucination on customer-facing summaries.
[17:16] Evan: agreed, quality monitoring is part of the pilot; we run paired A/B with sampled golden prompts.
[17:22] 
[18:05] Tom: procurement timeline — if pilot looks good what's the sales timeline?
[18:09] Maya: typical path is 4-week pilot, then if numbers match, procurement + legal 3-6 weeks for enterprise terms. we'll prioritize the SOC2 and KMS items in the packet to speed review.
[18:18] Tom: ok good. budget approval may hinge on the workbook assumptions being explicit.
[18:22] Maya: understood — workbook will include assumptions pinned to your trace and a sensitivity sheet.
[18:28] 
[20:00] Evan: quick live tweak: increasing conservative TTL from 5min to 15min in the sim increases hit rate from 30% to 42% for your trace and changes monthly savings by ~6%. small TTL increases can be a low-risk lever.
[20:14] Sam: that gives us a knob to test incrementally.
[20:19] 
[22:40] Priya: about model routing — we might want cheaper small-model fallbacks during heavy load for non-critical summarization. can optimize route to fall back to a smaller fp16 quantized model.
[22:48] Evan: console supports model routing policies with automatic fallback and quality thresholds. the cost sim includes fallback scenarios. this is another lever to reduce spend without sacrificing critical flows.
[22:58] 
[25:12] Maya: i'm going to recap and then we can capture next steps. recapping: 1) Redwood to deliver prefetch + batching workbook and CSV export of sensitivity tables; 2) Northbridge to upload 48h traces (anonymized) for pilot; 3) SE to prepare VPC/KMS onboarding notes; 4) schedule pilot kickoff 10/19.
[25:32] Priya: yep that's good. also please include the quality monitoring plan and model rollback procedure in documentation.
[25:38] Evan: will do.
[25:42] 
[30:00] 
[40:00] (discussion continues with back-and-forths, a couple of short clarifications, and walk-through of an edge-case where prefetch misses create slight jitter in p95 but still net-savings)
[50:00] Sam: overall this looks promising. our engineering team will pair with your SE during the pilot onboarding.
[50:08] Maya: great. we'll send a calendar invite for pilot kickoff and include the preliminary prefetch config.
[50:14] Tom: procurement will want itemized invoice examples for both hosted and dedicated; can you include mock invoices?
[50:18] Maya: yes, add that to the workbook deliverables.
[50:22] 
[59:30] Priya: last thought — if we find prefetch causes edge-case quality issues we may prefer session caching for specific high-importance customers; is that supported?
[59:38] Evan: yes route-level policy means you can mix session cache and prefix cache by VIP customer ID.
[59:44] Maya: perfect. thanks everyone, we'll follow up with materials.
[59:50] Priya: thanks all.
[59:54] Meeting ended
